entries.f3e6ea7897a4236952f73a81f3f9aa17e8e36702: <div sID="gen32210" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="1Thess.4" sID="1Thess.4"/> <div eID="gen32210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32211" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32212" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle gives earnest exhortations to abound in holiness, with a caution against uncleanness, enforced with several arguments, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.1-1Thess.4.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. He then mentions the great duties of brotherly love, and quietness with industry in our callings, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.9-1Thess.4.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. And concludes with comforting those who mourned for their relations and friends that died in the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13-1Thess.4.18">ver. 13-18</reference>.
entries.240dad6386e738cbe3958365ef4853727e31c1cf: <div eID="gen32212" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32211" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations to Holiness; Caution against Impurity. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32213" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Furthermore then we beseech you, brethren, and exhort <hi type="italic">you</hi> by the Lord Jesus, that as ye have received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, <hi type="italic">so</hi> ye would abound more and more. <hi type="super">2</hi> For ye know what commandments we gave you by the Lord Jesus. <hi type="super">3</hi> For this is the will of God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication: <hi type="super">4</hi> That every one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour; <hi type="super">5</hi> Not in the lust of concupiscence, even as the Gentiles which know not God: 6 That no <hi type="italic">man</hi> go beyond and defraud his brother in <hi type="italic">any</hi> matter: because that the Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified. <hi type="super">7</hi> For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness. 8 He therefore that despiseth, despiseth not man, but God, who hath also given unto us his holy Spirit. <div eID="gen32213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32214" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen32214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32215" type="x-p"/> I. An exhortation to abound in holiness, to <hi type="italic">abound more and more</hi> in that which is good, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.1-1Thess.4.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. We may observe, <div eID="gen32215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32216" type="x-p"/> 1. The manner in which the exhortation is given—very affectionately. The apostle entreats them as brethren; he calls them so, and loved them as such. Because his love to them was very great, he exhorts them very earnestly: <hi type="italic">We beseech and exhort you.</hi> The apostle was unwilling to take any denial, and therefore repeats his exhortation again and again. <div eID="gen32216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32217" type="x-p"/> 2. The matter of his exhortation—that they would abound more and more in holy walking, or excel in those things that are good, in good works. Their faith was justly famed abroad, and they were already examples to other churches: yet the apostle would have them yet further to excel others, and to make further progress in holiness. Note, (1.) Those who most excel others fall short of perfection. The very best of us should <hi type="italic">forget those things which are behind, and reach forth unto those things which are before.</hi> (2.) It is not enough that we abide in the faith of the gospel, but we must abound in the work of faith. We must not only persevere to the end, but we should grow better, and walk more evenly and closely with God. <div eID="gen32217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32218" type="x-p"/> 3. The arguments with which the apostle enforces his exhortation. (1.) They had been informed of their duty. They knew their Master's will, and could not plead ignorance as an excuse. Now as faith, so knowledge, is dead without practice. They had received of those who had converted them to Christianity, or been taught of them, <hi type="italic">how they ought to walk.</hi> Observe, The design of the gospel is to teach men not only what they should believe, but also how they ought to live; not so much to fill men's minds with notions as to regulate their temper and behaviour. The apostle taught them how to walk, not how to talk. To talk well without living well will never bring us to heaven: for the character of those who are in Christ Jesus is this: <hi type="italic">They walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.</hi> (2.) Another argument is that the apostle taught and exhorted them in the name, or by the authority, of the Lord Jesus Christ. He was Christ's minister and ambassador, declaring to them what was the will and command of the Lord Jesus. (3.) Another argument is this. Herein they would please God. Holy walking is most pleasing to the holy God, <hi type="italic">who is glorious in holiness.</hi> This ought to be the aim and ambition of every Christian, to please God and to be accepted of him. We should not be men-pleasers, nor flesh-pleasers, but should walk so as to please God. (4.) The rule according to which they ought to walk and act—<hi type="italic">the commandments they had given them by the Lord Jesus Christ,</hi> which were the commandments of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, because given by authority and direction from him and such as were agreeable to his will. The apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ were only commissioned by him to teach men to observe all things <hi type="italic">whatsoever he had commanded them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>. Though they had great authority from Christ, yet that was to teach men what Christ had commanded, not to give forth commandments of their own. They did not act as lords over God's heritage (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.3">1 Pet. v. 3</reference>), nor should any do so that pretend to be their successors. The apostle could appeal to the Thessalonians, who knew what commandments he gave them, that they were no other than what he had received from the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen32218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32219" type="x-p"/> II. A caution against uncleanness, this being a sin directly contrary to sanctification, or that holy walking to which he so earnestly exhorts them. This caution is expressed, and also enforced by many arguments, <div eID="gen32219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32220" type="x-p"/> 1. It is expressed in these words: <hi type="italic">That you should abstain from fornication</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.3">v. 3</reference>), by which we are to understand all uncleanness whatsoever, either in a married or unmarried state. Adultery is of course included, though fornication is particularly mentioned. And other sorts of uncleanness are also forbidden, of which it is a shame even to speak, though they are done by too many in secret. All that is contrary to chastity in heart, speech, and behaviour, is contrary to the command of God in the decalogue, and contrary to that holiness which the gospel requires. <div eID="gen32220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32221" type="x-p"/> 2. There are several arguments to enforce this caution. As, (1.) This branch of sanctification in particular is the will of God, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.3">v. 3</reference>. It is the will of God in general that we should be holy, because <hi type="italic">he that called us is holy,</hi> and because we are <hi type="italic">chosen unto salvation through the sanctification of the Spirit;</hi> and not only does God require holiness in the heart, but also purity in our bodies, and that we should cleanse ourselves from all <hi type="italic">filthiness both of flesh and spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2 Cor. vii. 1</reference>. Whenever the body is, as it ought to be, devoted to God, and dedicated and set apart for him, it should be kept clean and pure for his service; and, as chastity is one branch of our sanctification, so this is one thing which God commands in his law, and what his grace effects in all true believers. (2.) This will be greatly for our honour: so much is plainly implied, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.4">v. 4</reference>. Whereas the contrary will be a great dishonour. <hi type="italic">And his reproach shall not be wiped away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.6.33">Prov. vi. 33</reference>. The body is here called the vessel of the soul, which dwells therein (so <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.5">1 Sam. xxi. 5</reference>), and it must be kept pure from defiling lusts. Every one should be careful in this matter, as he values his own honour and will not be contemptible on this account, that his inferior appetites and passions gain not the ascendant, tyrannizing over his reason and conscience, and enslaving the superior faculties of his soul. What can be more dishonourable than for a rational soul to be enslaved by bodily affections and brutal appetites? (3.) To indulge the lust of concupiscence is to live and act like heathens? <hi type="italic">Even as the Gentiles who know not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.5">v. 5</reference>. The Gentiles, and especially the Grecians, were commonly guilty of some sins of uncleanness which were not so evidently forbidden by the light of nature. But they did not know God, nor his mind and will, so well as Christians know, and should know, this his will, namely <hi type="italic">our sanctification</hi> in this branch of it. It is not so much to be wondered at, therefore, if the Gentiles indulge their fleshly appetites and lusts; but Christians should not walk as unconverted Gentiles, <hi type="italic">in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings,</hi> &c. (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1 Pet. iv. 3</reference>), because those who are in Christ <hi type="italic">have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts.</hi> (4.) The sin of uncleanness, especially adultery, is a great piece of injustice that God will be the avenger of; so we may understand those words, <hi type="italic">That no man go beyond or defraud his brother</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">in any matter</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en to pragmati,</hi></hi> in <hi type="italic">this</hi> matter of which the apostle is speaking in the preceding and following verses, namely, the sin of uncleanness. Some understand these words as a further warning and caution against injustice and oppression, all fraud and deceit in our dealings with men, which are certainly criminal, and contrary to the gospel. And Christians should not impose upon the ignorance and necessity of those they deal with, and so go beyond them, nor should they by equivocations or lying arts defraud them; and although this may be practised by some and lie long undiscovered, and so go unpunished among men, yet the righteous God will render a recompence. But the meaning may rather be to show the injustice and wrong that in many cases are done by the sin of uncleanness. Not only are fornication and other acts of uncleanness sins against his own body who commits them (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.18">1 Cor. vi. 18</reference>), not only are they very injurious to the sinner himself both in soul and body, but sometimes they are very injurious, and no less than defrauding, acts of injustice to others, particularly to those who are joined together in the marriage covenant and to their posterity. And, as this sin is of such a heinous nature, so it follows that God will be the avenger of it. <hi type="italic">Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">Heb. xiii. 4</reference>. This the apostle had forewarned and testified by his gospel, which, as it contained exceedingly great and precious promises, so also it <hi type="italic">revealed from heaven the wrath of God against all ungodliness and unrighteousness among men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.18">Rom. i. 18</reference>. (5.) The sin of uncleanness is contrary to the nature and design of our Christian calling: <hi type="italic">For God hath called us not unto uncleanness, but unto holiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.7">v. 7</reference>. The law of God forbids all impurity, and the gospel requires the greatest purity; it calls us from uncleanness unto holiness. (6.) The contempt therefore of God's law and gospel is the contempt of God himself: <hi type="italic">He that despises despises God, not man</hi> only. Some might possibly make light of the precepts of purity and holiness, because they heard them from men like themselves; but the apostle lets them know that they were God's commands, and to violate them was no less than to despise God. He adds, <hi type="italic">God hath given Christians his Spirit,</hi> intimating that all sorts of uncleanness do in an especial manner grieve the Holy Spirit, and will provoke him to withdraw from us; and also the Holy Spirit is given unto us to arm us against these sins, and to help us to mortify these deeds of the body, that we may live, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.13">Rom. viii. 13</reference>.
entries.3fe3bca8f01501e0c5b4f4a81e97c984bc4257a7: <div eID="gen32221" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Brotherly Love. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32222" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> But as touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another. <hi type="super">10</hi> And indeed ye do it toward all the brethren which are in all Macedonia: but we beseech you, brethren, that ye increase more and more; <hi type="super">11</hi> And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you; <hi type="super">12</hi> That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> ye may have lack of nothing. <div eID="gen32222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32223" type="x-p"/> In these words the apostle mentions the great duties, <div eID="gen32223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32224" type="x-p"/> I. Of brotherly love. This he exhorts them to increase in yet more and more. The exhortation is introduced, not with a compliment, but with a commendation, because they were remarkable in the exercise of it, which made it less needful that he should write to them about it, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.9">v. 9</reference>. Thus by his good opinion of them he insinuated himself into their affections, and so made way for his exhortation to them. Note, We should take notice of that in others which is good, to their praise, that by so doing we may lay engagements upon them to abound therein more and more. Observe, <div eID="gen32224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32225" type="x-p"/> 1. What it is that the apostle commends in them. It was not so much their own virtue as God's grace; yet he takes notice of the evidence they gave of the grace of God in them. (1.) It was God's grace that he took special notice of: that God had taught them this good lesson: <hi type="italic">You yourselves are taught of God to love one another,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.9">v. 9</reference>. Whoever does that which is good is taught of God to do it, and God must have the glory. All who are savingly taught of God are taught this lesson, to love one another. This is the livery of Christ's family. Note also, The teaching of the Spirit exceeds the teaching of men; and, as no man should teach contrary to what God teaches, so none can teach so effectually as he teaches; and men's teaching is fain and useless unless God teach also. (2.) The Thessalonians gave good evidence of their being taught of God by <hi type="italic">their love to the brethren in all Macedonia,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.10">v. 10</reference>. They not only loved those of their own city and society, or such as were near them and just of their own sentiments, but their love was extensive. And a true Christian's is so to all the saints, though distant from him in place, and differing from him in some opinions or practices of less moment. <div eID="gen32225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32226" type="x-p"/> 2. The exhortation itself is to increase more and more in this great grace and duty of brotherly love, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.10">v. 10</reference>. Though these Thessalonians had in some sense no need of an exhortation to brotherly love, as if it were wholly wanting, yet they must be exhorted to pray for more, and labour for more. There are none on this side heaven who love in perfection. Those who are eminent in this or any other grace have need of increase therein as well as of perseverance unto the end. <div eID="gen32226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32227" type="x-p"/> II. Of quietness and industry in their callings. Observe, 1. The apostle exhorts to these duties: that they should <hi type="italic">study to be quiet,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.11">v. 11</reference>. It is the most desirable thing to have a calm and quiet temper, and to be of a peaceable and quiet behaviour. This tends much to our own and others' happiness; and Christians should study how to be quiet. We should be ambitious and industrious how to be calm and quiet in our minds, in patience to possess our own souls, and to be quiet towards others; or of a meek and mild, a gentle and peaceable disposition, not given to strife, contention, or division. Satan is very busy to disquiet us; and we have that in our own hearts that disposes us to be disquiet; therefore let us study to be quiet. It follows, <hi type="italic">Do your own business.</hi> When we go beyond this, we expose ourselves to a great deal of inquietude. Those who are busy-bodies, meddling in other men's matters, generally have but little quiet in their own minds and cause great disturbances among their neighbours; at least they seldom mind the other exhortation, to be diligent in their own calling, <hi type="italic">to work with their own hands;</hi> and yet this was what the apostle commanded them, and what is required of us also. Christianity does not discharge us from the work and duty of our particular callings, but teaches us to be diligent therein. 2. The exhortation is enforced with a double argument; namely, (1.) So we shall live creditably. Thus we shall walk honestly, or decently and creditably, towards those that are without, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.12">v. 12</reference>. This will be to act as becomes the gospel, and will gain a good report from those that are strangers, yea, enemies to it. Note, It is a great ornament to religion when the professors of it are of meek and quiet spirits, diligent to do their own business, and not busy-bodies in other men's matters. (2.) We shall live comfortably, and have lack of nothing, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.12">v. 12</reference>. People often by their slothfulness bring themselves into narrow circumstances, and reduce themselves to great straits, and are liable to many wants, when such as are diligent in their own business live comfortably and have lack of nothing. They are not burdensome to their friends, nor scandalous to strangers. They earn their own bread, and have the greatest pleasure in so doing.
entries.5d4935fb03a712cf40a8bbdbed85dff694bfcd13: <div eID="gen32227" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">State of Departed Saints. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 51.)</title> <div sID="gen32228" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. <hi type="super">14</hi> For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him. <hi type="super">15</hi> For this we say unto you by the word of the Lord, that we which are alive <hi type="italic">and</hi> remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep. 16 For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: <hi type="super">17</hi> Then we which are alive <hi type="italic">and</hi> remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord. <hi type="super">18</hi> Wherefore comfort one another with these words. <div eID="gen32228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32229" type="x-p"/> In these words the apostle comforts the Thessalonians who mourned for the death of their relations and friends that died in the Lord. His design is to dissuade them from excessive grief, or inordinate sorrow, on that account. <hi type="italic">All grief</hi> for the death of friends is far from being unlawful; we may weep at least for ourselves if we do not weep for them, weep for own loss, though it may be their fain. Yet we must not be immoderate in our sorrows, because, <div eID="gen32229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32230" type="x-p"/> I. This looks as if we had no hope, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">v. 13</reference>. It is to act too much like the Gentiles, who had no hope of a better life after this; whereas we Christians, who have a most sure hope, the hope of eternal life after this, <hi type="italic">which God who cannot lie hath promised us,</hi> should moderate all our joys and our sorrows on account of any worldly thing. This hope is more than enough to balance all our griefs upon account of any of the crosses of the present time. <div eID="gen32230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32231" type="x-p"/> II. This is an effect of ignorance concerning those who are dead, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">v. 13</reference>. There are some things which we cannot be ignorant of concerning those that are asleep; for the land they are removed to is a land of darkness, which we know but little of and have no correspondence with. To go among the dead is to go among we know not whom, and to live we know not how. Death is an unknown thing, and the state of the dead, or the state after death, we are much in the dark about; yet there are some things concerning those especially who die in the Lord that we need not, and ought not, to be ignorant of; and, if these things be really understood and duly considered, they will be sufficient to allay our sorrow concerning them. <div eID="gen32231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32232" type="x-p"/> 1. They sleep in Jesus. They are asleep, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">v. 13</reference>. They have <hi type="italic">fallen asleep in Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.18">1 Cor. xv. 18</reference>. Death does not annihilate them. It is but a sleep to them. It is their rest, and undisturbed rest. They have retired out of this troublesome world, to rest from all their labours and sorrows, and they sleep in Jesus, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">v. 14</reference>. Being still in union with him, they sleep in his arms and are under his special care and protection. Their souls are in his presence, and their dust is under his care and power; so that they are not lost, nor are they losers, but great gainers by death, and their removal out of this world is into a better. <div eID="gen32232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32233" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall be raised up from the dead, and awakened out of their sleep, for <hi type="italic">God will bring them with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">v. 14</reference>. They then are with God, and are better where they are than when they were here; and when God comes he will bring them with him. The doctrine of the resurrection and the second coming of Christ is a great antidote against the fear of death and inordinate sorrow for the death of our Christian friends; and this doctrine we have a full assurance of, because we <hi type="italic">believe that Jesus died and rose again,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.14">v. 14</reference>. It is taken for granted that as Christians they knew and believed this. The death and resurrection of Christ are fundamental articles of the Christian religion, and give us hope of a joyful resurrection; for <hi type="italic">Christ, having risen from the dead, has become the first fruits of those that slept;</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">those who have fallen asleep in him have not perished nor are lost,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.18">1 Cor. xv. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">20</reference>. His resurrection is a full confirmation of all that is said in the gospel, or by the word of the Lord, which has <hi type="italic">brought life and immortality to light.</hi> <div eID="gen32233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32234" type="x-p"/> 3. Their state and condition shall be glorious and happy at the second coming of Christ. This the apostle informs the Thessalonians of <hi type="italic">by the word of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.15">v. 15</reference>), by divine revelation from the Lord Jesus; for though the resurrection of the dead, and a future state of blessedness, were part of the creed of the Old-Testament saints, yet they are much more clearly revealed in and by the gospel. By this word of the Lord we know, (1.) That the Lord Jesus will come down from heaven in all the pomp and power of the upper world (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout.</hi> He ascended into heaven after his resurrection, and passed through these material heavens into the third heaven, which must retain him till the restitution of all things; and then he will come again, and appear in his glory. He will descend from heaven into this our air, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">v. 17</reference>. The appearance will be with pomp and power, <hi type="italic">with a shout</hi>—the shout of a king, and the power and authority of a mighty king and conqueror, with <hi type="italic">the voice of the archangel;</hi> an innumerable company of angels will attend him. Perhaps <hi type="italic">one,</hi> as general of those hosts of the Lord, will give notice of his approach, and the glorious appearance of this great Redeemer and Judge will be proclaimed and ushered in by the <hi type="italic">trump of God. For the trumpet shall sound,</hi> and this will awaken those that sleep in the dust of the earth, and will summon all the world to appear. For, (2.) The dead shall be raised: <hi type="italic">The dead in Christ shall rise first</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">v. 16</reference>), before those who are <hi type="italic">found alive at Christ's coming shall be changed;</hi> and so it appears that those who shall then <hi type="italic">be found alive shall not prevent those that are asleep,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.15">v. 15</reference>. The first care of the Redeemer in that day will be about his dead saints; he will raise them before the great change passes on those that shall be found alive: so that those who did not sleep in death will have no greater privilege or joy at that day than those who fell asleep in Jesus. (3.) Those that shall be found alive will then be changed. They shall <hi type="italic">be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">v. 17</reference>. At, or immediately before, this rapture into the clouds, those who are alive will undergo a mighty change, which will be equivalent to dying. This change is so mysterious that we cannot comprehend it: we know little or nothing of it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1 Cor. xv. 51</reference>. Only, in the general, <hi type="italic">this mortal must put on immortality,</hi> and these bodies will be made fit to inherit the kingdom of God, which flesh and blood in its present state are not capable of. This change will be <hi type="italic">in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.52">1 Cor. xv. 52</reference>), in the very instant, or not long after the raising up of those that sleep in Jesus. And those who are raised, and thus changed, shall meet together in the clouds, and there meet with their Lord, to congratulate him on his coming, to receive the crown of glory he will then bestow upon them, and to be assessors with him in judgment, approving and applauding the sentence he will then pass upon the prince of the power of the air, and all the wicked, who shall be doomed to destruction with the devil and his angels. (4.) Here is the bliss of the saints at that day: they shall <hi type="italic">be ever with the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">v. 17</reference>. It will be some part of their felicity that all the saints shall meet together, and remain together for ever; but the principal happiness of heaven is this, <hi type="italic">to be with the Lord,</hi> to see him, live with him, and enjoy him, for ever. This should comfort the saints upon the death of their friends, that, although death has made a separation, yet their souls and bodies will meet again; we and they shall meet together again: we and they shall meet together again: we and they with all the saints shall meet our Lord, and be with him for ever, no more to be separated wither from him or from one another for ever. And the apostle would have us <hi type="italic">comfort one another with these words,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.18">v. 18</reference>. We should endeavour to support one another in times of sorrow, not deaden one another's spirits, nor weaken one another's hands, but should comfort one another; and this may be done by serious consideration and discourse on the many good lessons to be learned from the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, the second coming of Christ, and the glory of the saints in that day.  <chapter eID="1Thess.4"/> <div eID="gen32234" type="x-p"/>

entries.190040afd2fceece44ced9eb284fafd73c93ed35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17963"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen36739" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.1-1Thess.4.18">1Th 4:1-18</reference>. Exhortations to Chastity; Brotherly Love; Quiet Industry; Abstinence from Undue Sorrow for Departed Friends, For at Christ's Coming All His Saints Shall Be Glorified.<div eID="gen36739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36740" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17963"/><hi type="bold">1. Furthermore--</hi>Greek, "As to what remains." Generally used towards the close of his Epistles (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.10">Ep 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Php 4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>with a view to the love and holiness (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.12">1Th 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.13">13</reference>) which we have just prayed for in your behalf, we now give you exhortation.<div eID="gen36741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beseech--</hi>"ask" as if it were a personal favor.<div eID="gen36742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by, &c.--</hi>rather as Greek, "IN the Lord Jesus"; in communion with the Lord Jesus, as Christian ministers dealing with Christian people [Edmunds].<div eID="gen36743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ye ... received--</hi>when we were with you (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">1Th 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how--</hi>Greek, the "how," that is, the manner.<div eID="gen36745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walk and ... please God--</hi>that is, "and so please God," namely, by your walk; in contrast to the Jews who "please not God" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1Th 2:15</reference>). The oldest manuscripts add a clause here, "even as also ye do walk" (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.10">1Th 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.11">5:11</reference>). These words, which he was able to say of them with truth, conciliate a favorable hearing for the precepts which follow. Also the expression, "abound more and more," implies that there had gone before a recognition of their already in some measure walking so. <div eID="gen36746" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6678e97b669729fca54c186502ed7b2ee7708a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17964"/><div sID="gen36747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17964"/><hi type="bold">2. by the Lord Jesus--</hi>by His authority and direction, not by our own. He uses the strong term, "commandments," in writing to this Church not long founded, knowing that they would take it in a right spirit, and feeling it desirable that they should understand he spake with divine authority. He seldom uses the term in writing subsequently, when his authority was established, to other churches. <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.10">1Co 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.17">11:17</reference>; and <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference> (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.18">1Th 4:18</reference>, where the subject accounts for the strong expression) are the exceptions. "The Lord" marks His paramount authority, requiring implicit obedience. <div eID="gen36747" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c60dd8891e196a242e266bf10baaf2b8903b5b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17965"/><div sID="gen36748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17965"/><hi type="bold">3. For--</hi>enforcing the assertion that his "commandments" were "by (the authority of) the Lord Jesus" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.2">1Th 4:2</reference>). Since "this is the will of God," let it be your will also.<div eID="gen36748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fornication--</hi>not regarded as a sin at all among the heathen, and so needing the more to be denounced (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.20">Ac 15:20</reference>). <div eID="gen36749" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ff912c32f12f5555bbdf644113e6eaa19ca1327: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17966"/><div sID="gen36750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17966"/><hi type="bold">4. know--</hi>by moral self-control.<div eID="gen36750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how to possess his vessel--</hi>rather as Greek, "how to acquire (get for himself) his own vessel," that is, that each should have his own wife so as to avoid fornication (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.3">1Th 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2">1Co 7:2</reference>). The emphatical position of "his own" in the Greek, and the use of "vessel" for wife, in <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1Pe 3:7</reference>, and in common Jewish phraseology, and the correct translation "acquire," all justify this rendering.<div eID="gen36751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in sanctification--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.6.19">Ro 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.15">1Co 6:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.18">18</reference>). Thus, "his own" stands in opposition to dishonoring his brother by lusting after his wife (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.6">1Th 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honour--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">He 13:4</reference>) contrasted with "dishonor their own bodies" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Ro 1:24</reference>). <div eID="gen36753" type="x-p"/>
entries.1eca693875dcc84263be445f5ce3f98e0956ee0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17967"/><div sID="gen36754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17967"/><hi type="bold">5. in the lust--</hi>Greek, "passion"; which implies that such a one is unconsciously the passive slave of lust.<div eID="gen36754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which know not God--</hi>and so know no better. Ignorance of true religion is the parent of unchastity (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.19">19</reference>). A people's morals are like the objects of their worship (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.26">De 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.8">Psa 115:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.23">Ro 1:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen36755" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec226f3b045c54cf9d0f17f9d68129eac59c7800: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17968"/><div sID="gen36756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17968"/><hi type="bold">6. go beyond--</hi>transgress the bounds of rectitude in respect to his "brother."<div eID="gen36756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defraud--</hi>"overreach" [Alford]; "take advantage of" [Edmunds].<div eID="gen36757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in any matter--</hi>rather as Greek, "in the matter"; a decorous expression for the matter now in question; the conjugal honor of his neighbor as a husband, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.4">1Th 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.7">1Th 4:7</reference> also confirms this view; the word "brother" enhances the enormity of the crime. It is your brother whom you wrong (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.6.27-Prov.6.33">Pr 6:27-33</reference>).<div eID="gen36758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>the coming Judge (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.7">2Th 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen36759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">avenger--</hi>the Righter.<div eID="gen36760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of all such--</hi>Greek, "concerning all these things;" in all such cases of wrongs against a neighbor's conjugal honor.<div eID="gen36761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testified--</hi>Greek, "constantly testified [Alford]. <div eID="gen36762" type="x-p"/>
entries.02cac4b4550b5a64ce07a06d08b56190001bcb04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17969"/><div sID="gen36763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17969"/><hi type="bold">7. unto uncleanness--</hi>Greek, "for the purpose of."<div eID="gen36763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto--</hi>rather as Greek, "in"; marking that "holiness" is the element in which our calling has place; in a sphere of holiness. Saint is another name for Christian. <div eID="gen36764" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1c2a4dd1a95a4215439c72adb8266b82eda7c2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17970"/><div sID="gen36765" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17970"/><hi type="bold">8. despiseth, &c.--</hi>Greek, "setteth at naught" such engagements imposed on him in his calling, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.7">1Th 4:7</reference>; in relation to his "brother," <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.6">1Th 4:6</reference>. He who doth so, "sets at naught not man (as for instance his brother), but God" (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.4">Psa 51:4</reference>) is used of despising or rejecting God's minister, it may mean here, "He who despiseth" or "rejecteth" these our ministerial precepts.<div eID="gen36765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who hath also given unto us--</hi>So some oldest manuscripts read, but most oldest manuscripts read, "Who (without 'also') giveth (present) unto you" (not "us").<div eID="gen36766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his Spirit--</hi>Greek, "His own Spirit, the Holy (One)"; thus emphatically marking "holiness" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.7">1Th 4:7</reference>) as the end for which the Holy (One) is being given. "Unto you," in the Greek, implies that the Spirit is being given unto, into (put "into" your hearts), and among you (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>). "Giveth" implies that sanctification is not merely a work once for all accomplished in the past, but a present progressive work. So the Church of England Catechism, "sanctifieth (present) all the elect people of God." "His own" implies that as He gives you that which is essentially identical with Himself, He expects you should become like Himself (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.16">1Pe 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.4">2Pe 1:4</reference>). <div eID="gen36767" type="x-p"/>
entries.2812f91818ddef7eac2c9c2a95453dd559970122: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17971"/><div sID="gen36768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17971"/><hi type="bold">9. brotherly love, &c.--</hi>referring here to acts of brotherly kindness in relieving distressed brethren. Some oldest manuscripts support English Version reading, "YE have"; others, and those the weightiest, read, "WE have." We need not write, as ye yourselves are taught, and that by God: namely, in the heart by the Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="John.6.45">Joh 6:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.11">He 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>, 27).<div eID="gen36768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to love--</hi>Greek, "with a view to," or "to the end of your loving one another." Divine teachings have their confluence in love [Bengel]. <div eID="gen36769" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc0b4b0006e43f6c7bc78b562439d5c6413c3aec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17972"/><div sID="gen36770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17972"/><hi type="bold">10. And indeed--</hi>Greek, "For even." <div eID="gen36770" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc0876e65304967ad308fc129cb2d73d5dc200d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17973"/><div sID="gen36771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17973"/><hi type="bold">11. study to be quiet--</hi>Greek, "make it your ambition to be quiet, and to do your own business." In direct contrast to the world's ambition, which is, "to make a great stir," and "to be busybodies" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.11">2Th 3:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen36771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work with your own hands--</hi>The Thessalonian converts were, it thus seems, chiefly of the working classes. Their expectation of the immediate coming of Christ led some enthusiasts among them to neglect their daily work and be dependent on the bounty of others. See end of <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.12">1Th 4:12</reference>. The expectation was right in so far as that the Church should be always looking for Him; but they were wrong in making it a ground for neglecting their daily work. The evil, as it subsequently became worse, is more strongly reproved in <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.6-2Thess.3.12">2Th 3:6-12</reference>. <div eID="gen36772" type="x-p"/>
entries.af318b21ceb46032007b02f6f5f8f39cd1cfeb08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17974"/><div sID="gen36773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17974"/><hi type="bold">12. honestly--</hi>in the Old English sense, "becomingly," as becomes your Christian profession; not bringing discredit on it in the eyes of the outer world, as if Christianity led to sloth and poverty (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.13">Ro 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.12">1Pe 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen36773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them ... without--</hi>outside the Christian Church (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.11">Mr 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have lack of nothing--</hi>not have to beg from others for the supply of your wants (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.28">Ep 4:28</reference>). So far from needing to beg from others, we ought to work and get the means of supplying the need of others. Freedom from pecuniary embarrassment is to be desired by the Christian on account of the liberty which it bestows. <div eID="gen36775" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1e398846b3de3a33930e4da2d42b3737d664999: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17975"/><div sID="gen36776" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17975"/>13. The leading topic of Paul's preaching at Thessalonica having been the coming kingdom (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.7">Ac 17:7</reference>), some perverted it into a cause for fear in respect to friends lately deceased, as if these would be excluded from the glory which those found alive alone should share. This error Paul here corrects (compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.10">1Th 5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen36776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I would not--</hi>All the oldest manuscripts and versions have "we would not." My fellow labourers (Silas and Timothy) and myself desire that ye should not be ignorant.<div eID="gen36777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them which are asleep--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read present tense, "them which are sleeping"; the same as "the dead in Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1Th 4:16</reference>), to whose bodies (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>, not their souls; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Ec 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.8">2Co 5:8</reference>) death is a calm and holy sleep, from which the resurrection shall waken them to glory. The word "cemetery" means a sleeping-place. Observe, the glory and chief hope of the Church are not to be realized at death, but at the Lord's coming; one is not to anticipate the other, but all are to be glorified together at Christ's coming (<reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.40">He 11:40</reference>). Death affects the mere individual; but the coming of Jesus the whole Church; at death our souls are invisibly and individually with the Lord; at Christ's coming the whole Church, with all its members, in body and soul, shall be visibly and collectively with Him. As this is offered as a consolation to mourning relatives, the mutual recognition of the saints at Christ's coming is hereby implied.<div eID="gen36778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ye sorrow not, even as others--</hi>Greek, "the rest"; all the rest of the world besides Christians. Not all natural mourning for dead friends is forbidden: for the Lord Jesus and Paul sinlessly gave way to it (<reference osisRef="John.11.31">Joh 11:31</reference>, 33, 35; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.27">Php 2:27</reference>); but sorrow as though there were "no hope," which indeed the heathen had not (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>): the Christian hope here meant is that of the resurrection. <reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Psa 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.24">73:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.32">Pr 14:32</reference>, show that the Old Testament Church, though not having the hope so bright (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.18">Is 38:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.19">19</reference>), yet had this hope. Contrast Catullus [Carmina 5.4], "When once our brief day has set, we must sleep one everlasting night." The sepulchral inscriptions of heathen Thessalonica express the hopeless view taken as to those once dead: as Aeschylus writes, "Of one once dead there is no resurrection." Whatever glimpses some heathen philosophers, had of the existence of the soul after death, they had none whatever of the body (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.18">Ac 17:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">20, 32</reference>). <div eID="gen36779" type="x-p"/>
entries.2465355b380146624fdf068659f882130b29b103: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17976"/><div sID="gen36780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17976"/><hi type="bold">14. For if--</hi>confirmation of his statement, <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>, that the removal of ignorance as to the sleeping believers would remove undue grief respecting them. See <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>, "hope." Hence it appears our hope rests on our faith ("if we believe"). "As surely as we all believe that Christ died and rose again (the very doctrine specified as taught at Thessalonica, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.3">Ac 17:3</reference>), so also will God bring those laid to sleep by Jesus with Him (Jesus)." (So the order and balance of the members of the Greek sentence require us to translate). Believers are laid in sleep by Jesus, and so will be brought back from sleep with Jesus in His train when He comes. The disembodied souls are not here spoken of; the reference is to the sleeping bodies. The facts of Christ's experience are repeated in the believer's. He died and then rose: so believers shall die and then rise with Him. But in His case death is the term used, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">1Co 15:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.6">6</reference>, &c.; in theirs, sleep; because His death has taken for them the sting from death. The same Hand that shall raise them is that which laid them to sleep. "Laid to sleep by Jesus," answers to "dead in Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1Th 4:16</reference>). <div eID="gen36780" type="x-p"/>
entries.16cfe07478a52d077913b377d92a8cbe995c7f3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17977"/><div sID="gen36781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17977"/><hi type="bold">15. by the word of the Lord--</hi>Greek, "in," that is, in virtue of a direct revelation from the Lord to me. So <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.35">1Ki 20:35</reference>. This is the "mystery," a truth once hidden, now revealed, which Paul shows (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.52">52</reference>).<div eID="gen36781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prevent--</hi>that is, "anticipate." So far were the early Christians from regarding their departed brethren as anticipating them in entering glory, that they needed to be assured that those who remain to the coming of the Lord "will not anticipate them that are asleep." The "we" means whichever of us are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord. The Spirit designed that believers in each successive age should live in continued expectation of the Lord's coming, not knowing but that they should be among those found alive at His coming (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.42">Mt 24:42</reference>). It is a sad fall from this blessed hope, that death is looked for by most men, rather than the coming of our Lord. Each successive generation in its time and place represents the generation which shall actually survive till His coming (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.13">Mt 25:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Ro 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.9">Jas 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1Pe 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.6">6</reference>). The Spirit subsequently revealed by Paul that which is not inconsistent with the expectation here taught of the Lord's coming at any time; namely, that His coming would not be until there should be a "falling away first" (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.2">2Th 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>); but as symptoms of this soon appeared, none could say but that still this precursory event might be realized, and so the Lord come in his day. Each successive revelation fills in the details of the general outline first given. So Paul subsequently, while still looking mainly for the Lord's coming to clothe him with his body from heaven, looks for going to be with Christ in the meanwhile (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1-2Cor.5.10">2Co 5:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.6">Php 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.20">3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.5">4:5</reference>). Edmunds well says, The "we" is an affectionate identifying of ourselves with our fellows of all ages, as members of the same body, under the same Head, Christ Jesus. So <reference osisRef="Hos.12.4">Ho 12:4</reference>, "God spake with us in Beth-el," that is, with Israel. "We did rejoice," that is, Israel at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.6">Psa 66:6</reference>). Though neither Hosea, nor David, was alive at the times referred to, yet each identifies himself with those that were present. <div eID="gen36782" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8adeab416386b667078ca6b5cd0725d3410f9ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17978"/><div sID="gen36783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17978"/><hi type="bold">16. himself--</hi>in all the Majesty of His presence in person, not by deputy.<div eID="gen36783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">descend--</hi>even as He ascended (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with--</hi>Greek, "in," implying one concomitant circumstance attending His appearing.<div eID="gen36785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shout--</hi>Greek, "signal shout," "war shout." Jesus is represented as a victorious King, giving the word of command to the hosts of heaven in His train for the last onslaught, at His final triumph over sin, death, and Satan (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.11-Rev.19.21">Re 19:11-21</reference>).<div eID="gen36786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the voice of ... archangel--</hi>distinct from the "signal shout." Michael is perhaps meant (Jude 9; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.7">Re 12:7</reference>), to whom especially is committed the guardianship of the people of God (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.13">Da 10:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trump of God--</hi>the trumpet blast which usually accompanies God's manifestation in glory (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">Ex 19:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference>); here the last of the three accompaniments of His appearing: as the trumpet was used to convene God's people to their solemn convocations (<reference osisRef="Num.10.2">Nu 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.10.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.31.6">31:6</reference>), so here to summon God's elect together, preparatory to their glorification with Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.1-Ps.50.5">Psa 50:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">Mt 24:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.52">1Co 15:52</reference>).<div eID="gen36788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall rise first--</hi>previously to the living being "caught up." The "first" here has no reference to the first resurrection, as contrasted with that of "the rest of the dead." That reference occurs elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">Mt 13:41</reference>, 42, 50; <reference osisRef="John.5.29">Joh 5:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">1Co 15:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.5">Re 20:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.6">6</reference>); it simply stands in opposition to "then," <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.17">1Th 4:17</reference>. FIRST, "the dead in Christ" shall rise, THEN the living shall be caught up. The Lord's people alone are spoken of here. <div eID="gen36789" type="x-p"/>
entries.ced7920646279bbcade32da50622a0a7505512f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17979"/><div sID="gen36790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17979"/><hi type="bold">17. we which are alive ... shall be caught up--</hi>after having been "changed in a moment" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.52">52</reference>). Again he says, "we," recommending thus the expression to Christians of all ages, each generation bequeathing to the succeeding one a continually increasing obligation to look for the coming of the Lord. [Edmunds].<div eID="gen36790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">together with them--</hi>all together: the raised dead, and changed living, forming one joint body.<div eID="gen36791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the clouds--</hi>Greek, "in clouds." The same honor is conferred on them as on their Lord. As He was taken in a cloud at His ascension (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.9">Ac 1:9</reference>), so at His return with clouds (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Re 1:7</reference>), they shall be caught up in clouds. The clouds are His and their triumphal chariot (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.3">Psa 104:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>). Ellicott explains the Greek, "robed round by upbearing clouds" [Aids to Faith].<div eID="gen36792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the air--</hi>rather, "into the air"; caught up into the region just above the earth, where the meeting (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">Mt 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">6</reference>) shall take place between them ascending, and their Lord descending towards the earth. Not that the air is to be the place of their lasting abode with Him.<div eID="gen36793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and so shall we ever be with the Lord--</hi>no more parting, and no more going out (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>). His point being established, that the dead in Christ shall be on terms of equal advantage with those found alive at Christ's coming, he leaves undefined here the other events foretold elsewhere (as not being necessary to his discussion), Christ's reign on earth with His saints (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.3">3</reference>), the final judgment and glorification of His saints in the new heaven and earth. <div eID="gen36794" type="x-p"/>
entries.478e6ee33b40d115990702dbed65d33e862a8407: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17980"/><div sID="gen36795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17980"/><hi type="bold">18. comfort one another--</hi>in your mourning for the dead (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.13">1Th 4:13</reference>). <chapter eID="1Thess.4"/>

entries.f06877d6b8505421d777fd6ae31e90d020868e5a: <div eID="gen51162" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51163" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51164" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51164" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51163" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51165" type="x-p"/> The apostle exhorts them to attend to the directions which he had already given them, that they might know how to walk and please God, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.1">1Thes 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.2">1Thes 4:2</reference>. Gives them exhortations concerning continence, chastity, and matrimonial fidelity, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.3-1Thes.4.8">1Thes 4:3-8</reference>. Speaks concerning their love to each other, and love to the Churches of Christ; and exhorts them to continue and increase in it, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.9">1Thes 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.10">1Thes 4:10</reference>. Counsels them to observe an inoffensive conduct, to mind their own affairs, to do their own business, and to live honestly, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.11">1Thes 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.12">1Thes 4:12</reference>. Not to sorrow for the dead, as persons who have no hope of a resurrection; because to Christians the resurrection of Christ is a proof of the resurrection of his followers, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.13">1Thes 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.14">1Thes 4:14</reference>. Gives a short but awful description of the appearing of Christ to judge the world, <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.15">1Thes 4:15</reference>. <div eID="gen51165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51166" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51167" type="x-p"/> We beseech you, brethren, and exhort - We give you proper instructions in heavenly things, and request you to attend to our advice. The apostle used the most pressing entreaties; for he had a strong and affectionate desire that this Church should excel in all righteousness and true holiness. <div eID="gen51167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51168" type="x-p"/> Please God more and more - God sets no bounds to the communications of his grace and Spirit to them that are faithful. And as there are no bounds to the graces, so there should be none to the exercise of those graces. No man can ever feel that he loves God too much, or that he loves man too much for God's sake.
entries.7819992c3dcd05cfe718c3582a8e637eaa1b3691: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51169" type="x-p"/> Ye know what commandments we gave you - This refers to his instructions while he was among them; and to instructions on particular subjects, which he does not recapitulate, but only hints at.
entries.fef5109bbb128cab01632dcfe8dae38c50bf02f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51170" type="x-p"/> This is the will of God, even your sanctification - God has called you to holiness; he requires that you should be holy; for without holiness none can see the Lord. This is the general calling, but in it many particulars are included. Some of these he proceeds to mention; and it is very likely that these had been points on which he gave them particular instructions while among them. <div eID="gen51170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51171" type="x-p"/> That ye should abstain from fornication - The word πορνεια, as we have seen in other places, includes all sorts of uncleanness; and it was probably this consideration that induced several MSS., some versions and fathers, to add here πασης, all. Directions of this kind were peculiarly necessary among the Greeks, and indeed heathens in general, who were strongly addicted to such vices.
entries.15cd3c12644c3bb5695beda5d64c505791851476: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51172" type="x-p"/> How to possess his vessel - Let every man use his wife for the purpose alone for which God created her, and instituted marriage. The word σκευοςanswers to the Hebrew כלי keli, which, though it signifies vessel in general, has several other meanings. That the rabbins frequently express wife by it, Schoettgen largely proves; and to me it appears very probable that the apostle uses it in that sense here. St. Peter calls the wife the weaker Vessel, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1Pet 3:7</reference>. Others think that the body is meant, which is the vessel in which the soul dwells. In this sense St. Paul uses it, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Cor 4:7</reference> : We have this treasure in earthen Vessels; and in this sense it is used by both Greek and Roman authors. There is a third sense which interpreters have put on the word, which I forbear to name. The general sense is plain; purity and continency are most obviously intended, whether the word be understood as referring to the wife or the husband, as the following verse sufficiently proves.
entries.232007c6bf88680a1a9dddfff94224830388e819: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51173" type="x-p"/> Not in the lust of concupiscence - Having no rational object, aim, nor end. Some say, "not like beasts;" but this does not apply as they who use it wish, for the males and females of the brute creation are regular and consistent in their intercourse, and scarcely ever exceed such bounds as reason itself would prescribe to those most capable of observing and obeying its dictates. <div eID="gen51173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51174" type="x-p"/> The Gentiles which know not God - These are the beasts; their own brutes are rational creatures when compared with them. Enough has been said on this subject on Romans 1, and 2: They who wish to see more may consult Juvenal, and particularly his 6th and 9th Satires; and indeed all the writers on Greek and Roman morals.
entries.7c860b1f1239f9f7df650ab256f5394fdab4d2b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51175" type="x-p"/> That no man go beyond and defraud his brother - That no man should by any means endeavor to corrupt the wife of another, or to alienate her affections or fidelity from her husband; this I believe to be the apostle's meaning, though some understand it of covetousness, overreaching, tricking, cheating, and cozenage in general. <div eID="gen51175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51176" type="x-p"/> The Lord is the avenger of all such - He takes up the cause of the injured husband wherever the case has not been detected by man, and all such vices he will signally punish. Every species of uncleanness was practised among the heathens, nor were they reputed as vices. Their gods, their emperors, their philosophers, and their great men in general, gave them examples of every species of impurity; and they had no system of ethics which forbade these abominations. The Christian religion not only discountenances these things, but forbids them on the most awful penalties; therefore wherever Christianity prevails, these vices, if practised at all, are obliged to seek the deepest gloom of midnight to cover them from the eyes of men. On this account they are comparatively rare, even among the mere professors of Christianity; they exist, but do not flourish.
entries.45034ab20e1b1394c09baf4eec7f670d20c309f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen51176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51177" type="x-p"/> God hath not called us unto uncleanness - He is the creator of male and female, and the institutor of marriage, and he has called men and women to this state; but the end of this and all the other callings of God to man is holiness, not uncleanness. And they who use the marriage state as he directs, will find it conducive to their holiness and perfection.
entries.f17dda65269ba1d08ee99f4cff342bb33a8dd7f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen51177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51178" type="x-p"/> He therefore that despiseth - He who will not receive these teachings, and is led either to undervalue or despise them, despises not us but God, from whom we have received our commission, and by whose Spirit we give these directions. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="1Thes.4.15">1Thes 4:15</reference>. <div eID="gen51178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51179" type="x-p"/> Hath also given unto us his Holy Spirit - Instead of εις ἡμας, unto Us, εις ὑμας, unto You, is the reading of BDEFG, a great many others, the Syriac, all the Arabic, Armenian, later Syriac in the margin, some of the Itala, Clement, Didymus, and Ambrosiaster; this seems to be the better reading. God has taught us that we may teach you; and he has also given you his Holy Spirit that ye might understand and be enabled to practice these things. It is one thing to receive a revelation from the Spirit of God; it is another thing to receive that Spirit to enable a man to live according to that revelation. In the first sense the apostles alone received this Holy Spirit; in the latter sense all true Christians, as well as the Thessalonians, receive it. I think ὑμας, you, is the true reading, and that it is confirmed by the following verse: For ye yourselves are Taught of God to love one another. Griesbach has inserted it in the margin, but has not admitted it into the text, because it has not what he deemed full support from those MSS. which are of the Alexandrian recension; but he thought its genuineness very probable.
entries.714dd15aa0aeb70bd812d503ba805d8b0167bd9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen51179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51180" type="x-p"/> Touching brotherly love - They were remarkable for this; and though the apostle appears to have had this as a topic on which he intended to write to them, yet, from the account which he received of their prosperous state by Timothy, he finds that it is unnecessary to spend any time in inculcating a doctrine which they fully understood and practised. See <reference osisRef="1Thes.3.6">1Thes 3:6</reference>.
entries.731ade9836d3b04c040a93cef405c98bd76c7818: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen51180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51181" type="x-p"/> Ye do it toward all the brethren - Ye not only love one another at Thessalonica, but ye love all the brethren in Macedonia; ye consider them all as children of the same Father; and that all the Churches which are in Christ make one great and glorious body, of which he is the head.
entries.0c5c2734bbdd1acee9e366a97b04a025004b73dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen51181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51182" type="x-p"/> That ye study to be quiet - Though in general the Church at Thessalonica was pure and exemplary, yet there seem to have been some idle, tattling people among them, who disturbed the peace of others; persons who, under the pretense of religion, gadded about from house to house; did not work, but were burdensome to others; and were continually meddling with other people's business, making parties, and procuring their bread by religious gossiping. To these the apostle gives those directions which the whole Church of God should enforce wherever such troublesome and dangerous people are found; viz.: That they should study to be quiet, ἡσυχαζειν, to hold their peace, as their religious cant will never promote true religion; that they should do their own business, and let that of others alone; and that they should work with their own hands, and not be a burden to the Church of God, or to those well meaning but weak and inconsiderate people who entertain them, being imposed on by their apparent sanctity and glozing conversation. An idle person, though able to discourse like an angel, or pray like an apostle, cannot be a Christian; all such are hypocrites and deceivers; the true members of the Church of Christ walk, work, and labor.
entries.9cebc74d2aeb3b3333e187d73322f10e5c932e0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen51182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51183" type="x-p"/> That ye may walk honestly - Ευσχημονως· Becomingly, decently, respectably; as is consistent with the purity, holiness, gravity, and usefulness of your Christian calling. <div eID="gen51183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51184" type="x-p"/> Them that are without - The unconverted Gentiles and Jews. See this expression explained at large on <reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>. <div eID="gen51184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51185" type="x-p"/> That ye may have lack of nothing - That ye may be able to get your bread by honest labor, which God will ever bless; and be chargeable to no man. He that is dependent on another is necessarily in bondage; and he who is able to get his own bread by the sweat of his brow, should not be under obligation even to a king. <div eID="gen51185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51186" type="x-p"/> I do not recollect whether, in any other part of this work, I have given the following story from the Hatem Tai Nameh. Hatem Tai was an Arabian nobleman, who flourished some time before the Mahommedan era; he was reputed the most generous and liberal man in all the east. One day he slew one hundred camels, and made a feast, to which all the Arabian lords and all the peasantry in the district were invited. About the time of the feast he took a walk towards a neighboring wood, to see if he could find any person whom he might invite to partake of the entertainment which he had then provided. Walking along the skirt of the wood, he espied an old man coming out of it, laden with a burden of faggots; he accosted him and asked if he had not heard of the entertainment made that day by Hatem Tai. The old man answered in the affirmative. He asked him why he did not attend and partake with the rest. The old man answered: "He that is able to gain his bread even by collecting faggots in the wood, should not be beholden even to Hatem Tai." This is a noble saying, and has long been a rule of conduct to the writer of this note.
entries.3fd64fd7da7c0cd8c2c7832cc1d68c90021f8deb: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen51186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51187" type="x-p"/> I would not have you to be ignorant - Instead of εχομεν, have, θελομεν, wish, is the reading of ADEFG, many others, besides the Arabic, Ethiopic, Armenian, some of the Slavonian, the Vulgate, and Itala, with many of the Greek fathers. This is undoubtedly the true reading: Brethren, I would not wish you to be ignorant; or, I would not that you should be ignorant. <div eID="gen51187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51188" type="x-p"/> This was probably one of the points which were lacking in their faith, that he wished to go to Thessalonica to instruct them in. <div eID="gen51188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51189" type="x-p"/> Them which are asleep - That is, those who are dead. It is supposed that the apostle had heard that the Thessalonians continued to lament over their dead, as the heathens did in general who had no hope of the resurrection of the body; and that they had been puzzled concerning the doctrine of the resurrection. To set them right on this important subject, he delivers three important truths: <div eID="gen51189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51190" type="x-p"/> 1. He asserts, as he had done before, that they who died in the Lord should have, in virtue of Christ's resurrection, a resurrection unto eternal life and blessedness. <div eID="gen51190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51191" type="x-p"/> 2. He makes a new discovery, that the last generation should not die at all, but be in a moment changed to immortals. <div eID="gen51191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51192" type="x-p"/> 3. He adds another new discovery, that, though the living should not die, but be transformed, yet the dead should first be raised, and be made glorious and immortal; and so, in some measure, have the preference and advantage of such as shall then be found alive. See Dodd.
entries.686fc0a813f27dd076432d01f19ce2829c62e38b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen51192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51193" type="x-p"/> For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again - Ει γαρ· Seeing that we believe; knowing that the resurrection of Christ is as fully authenticated as his death. <div eID="gen51193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51194" type="x-p"/> Even so them - It necessarily follows that them who sleep - die, in him - in the faith of the Gospel, will God bring with him - he will raise them up as Jesus was raised from the dead, in the same manner, i.e. by his own eternal power and energy; and he will bring them with him - with Christ, for he is the head of the Church, which is his body.
entries.ff7bad51b987615b9b476a10b34be6ced589b0f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen51194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51195" type="x-p"/> This we say unto you by the word of the Lord - This I have, by express revelation, from the Lord: what he now delivers, he gives as coming immediately from the Spirit of God. Indeed, human reason could not have found out the points which he immediately subjoins; no conjectures could lead to them. Allowing even the general doctrine of the resurrection to be believed, yet what follows does not flow from the premises; they are doctrines of pure revelation, and such as never could have been found out by human ingenuity. In no place does the apostle speak more confidently and positively of his inspiration than here; and we should prepare ourselves to receive some momentous and interesting truth. <div eID="gen51195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51196" type="x-p"/> We which are alive, and remain - By the pronoun we the apostle does not intend himself, and the Thessalonians to whom he was then writing; he is speaking of the genuine Christians which shall be found on earth when Christ comes to judgment. From not considering the manner in which the apostle uses this word, some have been led to suppose that he imagined that the day of judgment would take place in that generation, and while he and the then believers at Thessalonica were in life. But it is impossible that a man, under so direct an influence of the Holy Spirit, should be permitted to make such a mistake: nay, no man in the exercise of his sober reason could have formed such an opinion; there was nothing to warrant the supposition; no premises from which it could be fairly deduced; nor indeed any thing in the circumstances of the Church, nor in the constitution of the world, that could have suggested a hint of the kind. The apostle is speaking of the thing indefinitely as to the time when it shall happen, but positively as to the Order that shall be then observed. <div eID="gen51196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51197" type="x-p"/> Shall not prevent them which are asleep - Those who shall be found living in that day, though they shall not pass through death, but be suddenly changed, shall not go to glory before them that are dead, for the dead in Christ shall rise first - they shall be raised, their bodies made glorious, and be caught up to meet the Lord, before the others shall be changed. And this appears to be the meaning of the apostle's words, μη φθασωμεν, which we translate shall not prevent; for, although this word prevent, from prae and venio, literally signifies to go before, yet we use it now in the sense of to hinder or obstruct. Φθανειν τινα signifies the same, according to Hesychius, as προηκειν, to go before, προλαμβανειν, to anticipate, be before. Those who shall be found alive on that day shall not anticipate glory before the dead in Christ; for they shall rise first, and begin the enjoyment of it before the others shall be changed. This appears to be the apostle's meaning.
